name: primer3
why: Real molecular biology software for designing PCR primers, a genuine scientific tool you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: Primer3 is a command-line C program, with Perl test scripts, that designs PCR primers from a DNA sequence. The core binary, primer3_core, reads Boulder-IO text records from stdin or a file. Each record gives a template sequence, optional target and exclusion regions, and PRIMER_ settings such as size, melting temperature, GC content and product size range. It prints ranked candidate primer pairs in the same Boulder-IO format, or a readable report when run with --format_output. The homepage says it can also design hybridization probes (internal oligos) and sequencing primers. The brew executables list also includes ntdpal, ntthal, oligotm, long_seq_tm_test, amplicon3_core and primer3_masker; the README names only primer3_core, ntdpal, oligotm and long_seq_tm_test.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes PCR as an essential and ubiquitous tool in genetics and molecular biology, and says PCR is used for many different goals, so primer3 exposes many input parameters that let the user define what makes a good primer for their goal. The README frames it as doing everything from mispriming libraries and sequence quality data to generating internal oligos.
brief.how_it_works: The manual says primer3 scores candidate primers against criteria including oligo melting temperature, size, GC content and primer-dimer possibilities, PCR product size, positional constraints within the template, and ectopic priming (amplifying the wrong sequence). Some criteria are hard constraints and others are terms in an objective function that defines the optimal pair. Thermodynamic alignment is used for oligo-oligo and hairpin checks by default from version 2.3 onward, and it needs parameter files from a primer3_config directory. The masker component (primer3_masker) masks template sequence before design.

brief.install_notes: Source build needs git, a C and C++ compiler (gcc/g++ in the README), make and cmake, plus perl for the tests. The manual says that if your perl is not called perl you must edit the test Makefile. Manual's Mac section describes a prebuilt bin folder copied into ~/bin or /usr/local/bin with optional PATH edits; the manual does not say how current that is. Windows needs Git for Windows, TDM-GCC MinGW (mingw32-make TESTOPTS=--windows) and ActivePerl, per the manual. Thermodynamic parameter files must sit in ./primer3_config/ or /opt/primer3_config/, or be pointed to with PRIMER_THERMODYNAMIC_PARAMETERS_PATH. No accounts, hardware or services are needed. The web interfaces Primer3Web and Primer3Plus are separate, per the manual.
brief.standout: It is a plain text-in, text-out tool with no account, GUI or service dependency, and it has been cited in the literature since 2012 with peer-reviewed papers in NAR and Bioinformatics. It also has a settings design that separates the same engine's defaults for a command-line user from those for a wet-lab web user, and its default settings changed in version 2.3 to use thermodynamic calculations.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage says 'last updated: 08.Jan.2022', the manual's copyright runs to 2022, and the Windows section points to tag v2.3.7. I did not see a release date or latest-commit date on the GitHub README, so I cannot confirm current activity. Brew lists it, so it is at least packaged.
brief.caveats: Windows build does not support the masker (primer3_masker); the manual says masker-related tests will fail there. Thermodynamic alignment depends on the primer3_config parameter files, and the manual warns that the path must be set correctly. The manual says it uses Boulder-IO tags, a pre-XML format, so scripting against it means learning that format. The manual warns that hard-coded Windows line endings break compilation and tests. Licensed GPL-2.0 or later, so programs that link to or include its code take on GPL terms. The manual and homepage look older in style and use plain http for the manual link. The homepage's 'last updated' date is from January 2022.
